CC-02

The spring’s life, in cycles

Every open is one cycle. A standard spring is rated for about 10,000.

Torsion springCC-02

Cycles10,000

Rated (std.)10,000

Broken · call · don’t lift it

Drawing · one torsion spring on its shaft, winding cone at left · wire, length and inside diameter get measured before we quote

  1. 0 cycles

    Wound to your door’s weight.

    A new spring is sized to the door, not to whatever happens to be on the truck. Too light and the opener does the lifting; too heavy and the door flies up.

  2. 5,000 cycles

    Four trips a day is about 1,460 cycles a year.

    Out to work, home, out for groceries, home. A standard spring is halfway through its life in under four years. You won’t hear it coming.

  3. 8,000 cycles

    Measured before we touch it.

    Wire size, length, inside diameter. All three go on the quote next to the cycle rating, so you can see what heavier wire buys you.

    “They measured the old spring before touching anything: wire size, length, inside diameter. The new pair is heavier wire, and the quote showed the cycle rating next to the price.”

    Agnieszka R., Parma Sample review

  4. 10,000 cycles

    Bang. Don’t lift the door.

    It goes on a cold morning, loud as a dropped shelf. If the spring above the door has a gap in it, don’t lift the door and don’t run the opener. Call. That’s the whole instruction.

    Torsion spring pair · $280–$450 Sample pricing

CC-06

Bottom section · the salt line

Road salt eats the bottom panel first.

Twenty winters of slush sit against the bottom section of a Cleveland door. When the panel is still made, we replace that one section and the seal. Not the door.

Bottom section replacement $400–$900 Sample pricing

Price it

“Bottom panel was rusted through from twenty winters of road salt. They replaced one section instead of the door and put a new seal on. No more leaves in the garage.”

Yvette H., Euclid Sample review
